title: Event cancellation: costs and insurance assessment
excerpt: Event cancellation in Moldova: recoverable costs, deposits, contracts and questions for assessing possible insurance without assuming availability.

seo.description: Organise event contracts, deposits, non-refundable costs and changes before assessing possible cancellation insurance in Moldova.

content:
Cancelling an event can leave the organiser with deposits, reserved equipment, contracted services and obligations towards participants. Insurance for those consequences cannot be assumed from the existence of a liability or property policy. For a company in the Republic of Moldova, assessment begins with the event programme, contracts and costs that cannot be recovered. Availability and accepted situations require separate confirmation.

This article helps an organiser prepare information for assessment. It does not confirm that ING Broker offers cancellation insurance for every event, promise payment of deposits or interpret legal clauses. Contractual decisions, obligations towards the public and disputes with a provider require specialist verification. An editorial preparation checklist does not replace that assessment.

Cancellation, postponement and interruption differ

Describe what would actually change in the programme. An event may never start, move to another date or stop after opening. Consequences and costs can differ. Ask for explanations of definitions in the documents considered rather than assuming the word cancellation covers every situation. Describe an organiser's commercial decision separately from an external circumstance.

Record who may decide on the change: the organising company, venue, partner or another relevant party. This article does not establish anyone's legal authority to terminate a contract. Identify the document describing each role and any unclear points. For several events in one programme, distinguish the effects on each date or location.

Separate recoverable and non-recoverable costs

Prepare a list of amounts paid, contractually committed and still unconfirmed. Separate venue rental, equipment, staff, transport, promotion and other relevant services. Do not place a paid expense and estimated future revenue in the same column. Insurance assessment needs explanations of each category, not merely the total budget approved internally.

For each cost, record whether the contract allows a refund, transfer to another date or reduction through an alternative solution. Do not assume a deposit is automatically lost or recoverable. Keep the agreement, invoice and provider's response. If a condition is unclear, mark it as a question rather than turning it into certain loss to complete the table.

The contracting calendar matters

Show when reservations were made, when instalments are paid and when programme-change decisions must be taken. Check these milestones before requesting a solution, not only after a problem occurs. Do not assume discussion begun after cancellation has been announced creates protection for already known costs. Describe the real circumstances completely and accurately.

For a multi-stage event, prepare a schedule of setup, opening and dismantling. An incident before public access can raise different questions from one during the programme. Request a clear description of the period being assessed and any conditions concerning changes. Do not promise colleagues that a new date automatically falls under the same documents without appropriate confirmation.

Venue and possible alternatives

Describe the premises, planned capacity and services supplied by the venue. State whether the event is indoors, outdoors or in both areas. Do not present an alternative venue as a certain solution unless its availability is confirmed. For internal planning, record which elements can move and which equipment depends on the original space.

This checklist does not certify venue safety or recommend opening to the public in unsuitable conditions. Technical checks, access arrangements and safety decisions belong to competent people. For insurance, communicate facts and known restrictions. A policy must not justify ignoring a warning or replace authorisation required for the activity.

Essential suppliers and dependencies

Identify providers without whom the programme cannot proceed as planned. Stage, sound, electricity, access, transport or other event-specific services may be relevant. Do not turn every supplier delay into an assumed accepted cause of loss. Ask which circumstances are considered and which documents would demonstrate the link between the problem and the event change.

Keep current contracts and operational contacts without publishing unnecessary personal details. Record any realistic alternative and the costs it would involve. A backup can reduce impact, but mentioning it here does not make it compulsory or contractually accepted. Check provider responses and what information must be communicated when a policy is assessed.

Weather does not automatically mean compensation

For an outdoor event, describe the actual exposure and prepared safety arrangements. Do not claim that every rainfall is covered. If a solution involving weather or another cause is discussed, request the relevant definitions, documents and limits. The forecast, conditions actually observed and decision to cancel are different pieces of information and must remain distinct.

This article gives no technical wind, temperature or rainfall thresholds for operating a stage. Such decisions belong to specialists and the documents applicable to the equipment and event. Keep the chronology and communications in the financial file. Do not retrospectively edit an explanation to fit an assumed policy condition. Accurate assessment begins with real facts.

Tickets and participants

Separate revenue received, amounts that may need refunding and the cost of administering refunds. Do not treat all planned income as certain loss. Seek appropriate legal review of conditions communicated to the public before publication or amendment. This article establishes no purchaser rights and does not justify refusing a ticket refund in a particular case.

Prepare an internal communication procedure and identify who confirms messages. Do not announce that an insurer will pay refunds before its decision. Incomplete information can cause confusion even where the organiser means well. Use participant information only for permitted purposes and through suitable channels, not in a public commercial form to demonstrate the event's size.

Comparing a possible insurance proposal

Read the subject, triggering events, period, limits and exclusions. The premium is the amount paid for insurance; the deductible is the share of a loss borne under the contract. Request explanations of cost categories and the calculation basis. Do not compare premiums alone if proposals concern different programmes, periods or accepted causes.

Ask about changes to venue, date, budget or suppliers and what information must be communicated. An organiser's internal message does not establish acceptance. Keep essential unclear conditions explicitly on the question list. Do not describe the proposal as complete protection or treat availability abroad as proof it can be intermediated for an event in Moldova.

Illustration: a conference moves dates

A company has a conference planned and learns the venue cannot host the programme on the agreed date. This example is illustrative, not a client case. The team collects the venue's answer and provider contracts, then separates services that can move from those needing renegotiation. The example creates no right to compensation or obligation to refund an amount.

Management prepares the cost breakdown and requests assessment of options. The insurance coordinator follows actual documents and the notification procedure where a relevant policy exists. Participant communication is prepared and checked separately. Organising a new date must neither hide documented losses nor turn every additional expense into an amount assumed payable by an insurer.

Useful assessment documents

  • Programme, date, venue and organiser role.
  • Costs and income separately, with estimates labelled.
  • Venue and essential-provider contracts.
  • Deposits, invoices and change or refund conditions.
  • Confirmed alternatives and their costs.
  • Known-problem and decision chronology.
  • Existing policy and unanswered questions.

Track changes after the first assessment

The event may change between the initial discussion and the actual day. A sponsor adds an activity, part moves outdoors or the stage supplier changes. Record the change date, approving person and effects on non-recoverable costs. Check conditions before assuming acceptance. An unchanged total budget is insufficient: the event's nature and dependencies may differ.

A decision register is useful even without a policy. If postponement becomes necessary, it helps explain what was paid, what can be recovered and which alternatives were considered. Separate that evidence from estimates of reputation or future sales. Do not automatically place reputational loss in the same total as a non-recoverable venue deposit.

Frequently asked questions about event cancellation

Does organiser liability insurance pay lost deposits?

Do not assume so. Liability towards other people and the financial consequences of cancellation are separate questions. Request explicit assessment of the cost categories and conditions available for the actual situation.

Does moving dates mean no loss?

A change of calendar alone does not establish this. Separate retained costs, recovered amounts and additional expenses, with supporting records. The method for assessing any loss depends on the relevant contract.

Can I seek insurance after knowing the event will not happen?

Disclose the real situation and do not assume retrospective protection for a known fact. This article does not confirm acceptance of such a request or recommend concealing information.

What before announcing cancellation?

Coordinate safety and operations with competent people and check contractual and communication implications. Do not promise unconfirmed insurer payments or deadlines.
